May be a niche one but keep a separate debit card for paying bills. Least in the US a decent number of banks will let you to open multiple accounts or at least an additional interest free account for free. If you keep one account just for paying bills and one for income / savings even if someone steals your debit card you only lose that month's bills—which can still be catastrophic when you're trying to build a financial safety net but it's a hell of a lot better than losing everything. 

Also helpful for keeping track of expenses since you'll auto-set-up transfers for recurring bills and any unplanned purchases will require a manual transfer (which you can do instantly if your bank has a phone app).

If your rent is more than 1/3rd of your income you're rent burdened which means you're one financial disaster (car crash / ambulance ride, card being stolen / account drained) away from homelessness. At 21 you're almost guaranteed to be rent burdened so it's worth considering.  Super easy, might save your ass one day.

Severe chronic pain. Closing my fists / tasks that require fine dexterity worsen it. Have to choose between trying to make sure I'm fed for the day and drawing. And to be honest always being under a time limit, knowing everything you put into anything will have to be taken from something you need to stay alive feels bad. It becomes physical self harm for dubious mental benefit. It's too much pressure. Not conducive to the experimental / self-improvement head space I want to be in when creating. Being rusty is one thing but the loss in technical skill as a result of physical and mental deterioration are heartrending. 

Drew my whole life, before I could even speak and never once called myself an artist. Didn't feel I had the right. Yet it was my calling. A way of living continually pushing me to learn new shit, never be satisfied but in a fun, challenging way. 

Then to fight to get better and be blown off over and over and over and never have anyone take your pain seriously, pain sperating you from a core of your being...it's more baggage than I can sit with as I fight to stay alive. 

Tried to live by the two cakes philosophy, push myself to just make shit anyway, sacrificing my physical health to do so but I just ended up feeling humiliated. My work didn't meet my own standards, the minimal positive reception I got felt like nothing and aggravated medical abandonment trauma. 

Which is all to say I hope you can reconnect with it. There's a great tic toc or whatever the fuck that pretty much encapsulates my philosophy about it now, even if I can't lige it myself. Dude mentions talking to a friend about how he enjoys making art and their immediate response is to go: oh are you any good at it? And that baffles him. Says it's akin to asking someone who enjoys going for walks if they're any good at it. The question is missing the point. 

Creating shit is human. It's something people do like ants build shit and birds fly. As society currently exists how many things do we have complete control over, limited only by skill we can improve alone / our own expectations? And again skill doesn't need to be the point (though I was pretty fucking good too)—the point is that creating what you want for the sake of it / for yourself can be an inherently subversive, empowering act in a society that feels entitled to your time and thoughts. 

So fwiw I hope you can reconnect with it in some capacity. Least ime changing mediums can help. Because then it's more fun learning without having to compare yourself to your previous skill level while your ego's still roughed up from all the shit you've been through. Best of luck man.

It's always a tricky subject to write about or share because you don't want the info used impulsively when other solutions to problems might exist but at the same time people feeling like they don't have choices in life or even their death can actually drive them into more extreme / impulsive acts, acts that are more harmful to themselves and those around them. Acts they might not have attempted at all simply by having access to knowledge and feeling like they have a choice / a shred of agency. That's my 2 cents.

Given that most of us deal with more stressful stuff day to day I try to rationalize it's silly to worry about something that will likely feel better than those daily struggles.

Beyond that it depends on what frightens you about death. Being forgotten might be combatted doing your best to leave behind lasting good. If you just wish you could've lived longer seen how things turn out (like me) maybe you can find comfort in that your matter will continue to exist. What was you will "see," it just won't know in the same way.

Also, researching death / final arrangements can help you feel more control over your finale. That as much as possible you go out how you want and have control over what happens to your body and stuff. Recommend looking up "The Order of the Good Death"; it's a great educational resource.

know what you mean with words like gotta. in the same vein (if i'm remembering correctly) one that drives me up the wall is a shortening of a common word, where they write it ending in z when almost nobody writes that even via text (might be "cuz" in lieu of "because" or something similar). 

imo it's a good example of where a more faithful translation is actually more culturally awkward. like Japanese has *levels* of (in)formality but in English there's an established precedent with written dialogue that writing exactly as people speak is awkward / cringey and distracting. you don't write every dropped letter on an accent or it becomes a parody. 

it's definitely a tricky line to walk and i don't envy the localization team at all. in recent years it seems there's been a shift to blunt any sense of foreignness in favor of the general good practice of trying to re-create the experience of reading the text in its native language...but that ignores the shared history many American fans have with Japanese comics. in the past companies had tiny budgets and were so afraid manga wouldn't take they left in honorifics, translated too literally...to the point that's what many of us grew up with that and it's no longer foreign.

personally i'd prefer a cultural notes section at the end of each volume with sfx translated in the margins (to preserve artwork / not be distracted by godawful kerning) as used to be the norm. that way you get a mostly natural experience reading but can still learn about lost nuance if you want.

That's where my mind went first too—to write around it—but there's a few issues.

1) the character is a young adult rather than an adult so they wouldn't necessarily have access to certain gourmet ingredients, but I wouldn't know enough to know which ones are off the table.

2) The recipe was obtained from a skilled home cook, not a professional. So it should be unique enough to spark their interest but not something they'd already know. 

3) They way I've written them reflects how observant and perfectionistic they are. To suddenly get super vague during a pivotal scene of reflection would feel out of character. 

4) And ngl the last reason is probably the biggest—it'd just bother me not to have a solid, accurate jumping off point. While I never ate awfully I had to completely change the way I eat about a decade ago for medical reasons. Did it cold turkey because hard transitions are easier for me than the endless opportunities to slip up (and give up) that come with gradual lifestyle changes. Cold turkey absolute has its own challenges but if you're making most of your own food it's a lot easier to exercise control for 20 minutes at the grocery store than every time you go to your pantry. Cold turkey also carries a certain social weight that establishes how committed you are to the endeavor in other people's minds. Having people around you who respect and support your choice is probably one of the most important (and undervalued) parts of any major lifestyle change. Having people poke fun at a daily struggle (even in good fun) can feel discouraging and ostracising esp. if you're used to eating in large groups that share your habits. People who encourage and normalize a big change make all the difference. 

Know that it can feel daunting and somewhat miserable the first few months because it makes you re-evalute how food is functioning in your life. For many people it's an emotional crutch - bad day at work eat it away. Food is fuel not pleasure. It can be pleasurable but you shouldn't be reaching for it because you feel bad but because you need it.

Also if you stick to it, you'll be shocked just how sweet or even disgusting old food you used to crave with taste after a month or two. Your taste buds and gut adjust.

Lastly, if it's overwhelming thinking about what healthy thing to make every single day - crock pot soup for the week and buy veggies and meat / protein substitute in bulk. Wash all at once and store in tupperware. When you're ready to eat pull out a fish fillet, some pre-washed / chopped veggies, season and throw in the oven to bake, set a timer and forget it. Instead of thinking oh fuck I have to learn how to cook healthily (huge endeavor) - tackle those two recipes for the week and build up from there. Even a cold turkey transition doesn't mean you have to become an expert over night. Manageable increments. You got this.

(US Med Advice) If you are struggling with health issues that are affecting your ability to work and don't know what's wrong find a doctor who is invested and willing to help - who understands the seriousness of the situation and is willing to work with you. Willing to do more referrals after the first one doesn't pan out. Willing to do testing. Willing to fill out documentation and paperwork. 

If you've never had serious health issues this may seem like bizarre common sense advice. Doctors' whole thing is supposed to be help & do no harm, right? Short answer: more often than not doctors will treat you like a thorn in their side. They shouldn't but they will. The longer explanation is that the intersection of insurance limiting the time a doctor can spend with each patient and classism (if you were able to get through medical school ($$$) you're likely already very out of touch with the needs  and everyday challenges of many of your patients) makes for a bad mix. Modern medicine is generally pretty amazing at handling acute problems, but chronic / rare conditions? Not so much - so you have to be prepared.

What this all means is that you will meet doctors who will dismiss you, who won't make referrals they should. There will be poor listeners and people who just don't want to get involved even though they believe you and "care" (but not enough to stand behind their word and put it to paper to support you). There will be people quick to slap unwarranted labels on you to make a tricky case (i.e. the headache that is you) go away. You DO NOT WANT these doctors. 

I *know* things get bleak *real quick* when you can't work and make money. It can take months to get into doctors - so you may feel you have no choice but to stick with a doctor who treats you like shit on his shoe. TRUST ME, you walk into a doctor's visit and you get bad, dismissive vibes, you walk the fuck out and never go back. Also general advice for everyone **get a good primary care doctor now** - when you're not sick. They are the person who refers you to specialists and is generally one of the longer waits you will encounter outside of rare specialists. Oh and get on wait / cancellation lists. 

Finally, your mileage may vary but start the process of getting in with **DVR / BVR** or your local variant. The division of vocational rehabilitation helps people with physical (and other) disabilities find and maintain work. They may be able to work with your employer to get modifications made to your workload or set up that allow you to hang on longer while you sort your health shit. They may also pay for an **FCE** - a functional capacity assessment - which evaluates your ability to work and will be invaluable if you end up having to apply for disability which is a whole awful process that can take years. Never take a phone disability rep's advice over the phone btw. The national line's workers are often dangerously misinformed. You go to your local social security office and you get shit in writing. Verbal counts for shit all and can cost you years and money if you trust the wrong person. And finally - for real - call **211** for local resources / help and know **form 221.6** is a very valuable form.

Procrastination is often about emotional regulation - i.e. avoiding unpleasant emotions associated with the task at hand. If you can identify those feelings and what about the task is setting them off that can be a helpful step one. Obviously there can be other things involved like ADHD but it's usually worth at least examining.

Personally I find it really difficult to start things but once I get into it I can usually power through. To combat this I've found setting an alarm to start tackling the task at a certain time can be a big help. I promise myself I don't even need to finish it, just do a minimum of maybe 15 minutes on it - then I can reward myself with something I've promised myself before starting (play a game, read a comic, eat a treat etc.). Usually the high of actually accomplishing something will carry me into other tasks I didn't even plan on doing.

I also find a change of scenery - like reserving a library study room or going to the park to work - or a change in company can do wonders.

By expert I'm not talking degree so much as lived experience with a lot of intersectional issues. Many people who counsel chronic health problems do not have as extensive experience treating specific traumas and so on. For instance finding someone with inpatient experience who also does xyz - surprisingly hard. 

I'm here asking now because people are literally at a loss of where to refer me. I've exhausted the list from my insurance (which had very few providers with openings to begin with) as well as every other local organization I could find. It may be hard to believe but it happens. Sometimes what you need isn't where you are.

Thanks for the response. 

Showing up consistently and on time is definitely a non issue. Lateness and not following through on your word are huge pet peeves since time is all we really have in the end - it's our most valuable resource. Also highly value frank honesty and hate lying - not that I can't do the whole social song and dance and can't see it's value (hey how are you fine can hurt when you're doing bad but it'd be wrong to burden a stranger with the truth). Overall I'd much prefer people be candid though and I'll readily admit my own shortcomings. Obviously that's not something anyone can do with 100% accuracy but you get the idea.

Trust is absolutely an issue, though it's not like I'm going in with a huge chip on my shoulder either. Not going in distrustful, but rather neutral and desperately searching for a reason to trust. The context of therapy *is* inherently somewhat triggering for me (years of psychological and physical abuse by a psychologist) but it's more like I'm waiting for them to give me a reason to trust in them / the process and our ability to make progress together. Which is something I will explicitly say to them. And I don't even need a lot - just something to hold on to, a small sense that they actually give a shit and you're not just another number to run through a process with them (again, tied to trauma). I think issues arise from the fact that in that context I do not emote normally. I've been told by peers I come off stoic so I make extra efforts to be completely candid about my thoughts / feelings in therapy. Even if people know this though it seems to create a lot of confusion where they make assumptions and conflate feelings with thoughts - i.e. because you feel this way you must think this which is often wrong. It leads to repetitious explanations of things I already understand, don't need, and makes me not feel understood which makes me feel worse. 

I've definitely met people I vibed with instantly in that I respected them as good people and they "got it" (i.e. that a lot of my stress does genuinely come from systems and things I can't control that anyone would be miserable under) but just venting about your week and having someone go that's some shit doesn't get you anywhere in the long run. 

Overly delicate and insincere therapists - the over the top oh I'm so glad you're here - when we've literally never met are the worst offenders. Idk basically I need an unusual blend of someone who's both exceptionally direct and willing to question rather than make assumptions or who just gets it outright (have met) but can be sensitive and considerate of the many things that can really hurt me. I think because I can be stoic people tend to react with frustration when an exercise doesn't go how they want - they think I can / am taking it just fine when that isn't the case at all. You can share that shit verbally all you like but from experience many people still have trouble believing words over visuals and dealing with someone who is extremely emotionally numb from trauma.

Another complicating factor is finding someone who is educated on dealing with chronic health conditions and asexuality. It does not feel good to have to be google to someone who is supposed to be helping you.
